answer:
**Shellac releases that feature John Coltrane on the personnel credits**  
(Discogs releases where Coltrane is listed as an instrumentalist and the format is shellac 10 ″ 78 RPM):

| Release | Record label / catalog | Release year | Side/track that lists Coltrane | Track that carries a *Written‑By* credit for Dizzy Gillespie |
|---------|------------------------|--------------|--------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| **Dizzy Gillespie And His Orchestra – “Tally‑Ho” / “I Can’t Remember”** | Telefunken Capitol – CL 839 | 1950 | Side A “Tally‑Ho” (Coltrane = alto saxophone, uncredited) | “Tally‑Ho” – *Written‑By – Dizzy Gillespie*【commentary 5†L11-L16】 |
| **Dizzy Gillespie And His Orchestra – “Coast To Coast” / “Oo‑la‑la”** | Telefunken Capitol – 450 | 1951 | Side A “Coast To Coast” (Coltrane = saxophone) & Side B “Oo‑la‑la” | “Coast To Coast” – *Written‑By – Buster Hardeng, D. Gillespie*; “Oo‑la‑la” – *Written‑By – Gillespie, Williams, Acea*【commentary 5†L18-L24】 |
| **Dizzy Gillespie – “Tin Tin Daeo” / “Birks Works”** | Dee Gee 3600 | 1951 | Side B “Birks Works” (Coltrane = tenor saxophone) | “Birks Works” – *Written‑By – Dizzy Gillespie*【commentary 5†L26-L30】 |

---

### Tracks for which **Dizzy Gillespie is credited as writer**

1. **Tally‑Ho** – from *Tally‑Ho / I Can’t Remember*  
2. **Coast To Coast** – from *Coast To Coast / Oo‑la‑la*  
3. **Oo‑la‑la** – from *Coast To Coast / Oo‑la‑la*  
4. **Birks Works** – from *Tin Tin Daeo / Birks Works*  

These are the only shellac records that satisfy the two criteria:

* Coltrane appears on the credit sheet (instrumentalist).  
* Gillespie receives a *Written‑By* (song‑writer) credit for at least one track on the release.

If you pull the releases directly from Discogs, you’ll find the same track‑writing credits in the “Track list / Credits” section of each release page.

Title: THE MAN WHO REFUSED TO LISTEN PAST 1933

We’re living in 1934. We just didn’t notice it.
Joe Bussard heard the shift in real time. That’s what made him unusual — not the collection, but the clarity. He sought out obscure 78-rpm records that otherwise would have disappeared — jazz, blues, bluegrass, country and folk recordings from the early 20th century — the history of America, pressed to shellac. He understood that once a sound disappears from living memory, it doesn’t come back. The record is all you have.
He founded a record label, Fonotone, in 1956 — the last commercial label to issue new recordings in the 78 RPM format. He recorded local musicians and made limited pressing runs, all without contracts, distribution deals, or profit. One of the artists he recorded early was John Fahey — a guitarist who would go on to become one of the most genuinely original voices in American music, precisely because he learned from the pre-radio stuff, the weird regional corners, the sounds that hadn’t been processed through the national broadcast machine.
Joe in his collection
Joe Bussard wasn’t just preserving records. He was preserving the proof that originality is possible — that music can come from a place, grow from a community, mean something specific rather than something general.
The resistance to monoculture is always local. Always stubborn. Always a little ornery.
Before radio, making something that sounded like nobody else was just called being a musician.
Joe Bussard drew his lines where he drew them. He died in 2022 with over 15,000 records and zero regrets. Even in his final year, fans visited his basement to hear records from his collection — and that meant a lot to him.
He loved people. He loved to connect people through music. He just thought music connected people better when it came from somewhere specific.
I don’t think he was wrong.

It tells my publisher and distributer that people like you care about books like this. ## A FEAST OF A BOOK: “MORE THAN THE MUSIC: A JAZZ MEMOIR by HANK O’NEAL” (TCU PRESS,2025)
A concert at Town Hall, November 28, 1959, with an extended performance of ONE O’CLOCK JUMP with Count Basie, John Coltrane, Milt Hinton, Elvin Jones, Lee Konitz, Bob Brookmeyer, and others.
Zoot Sims’ advice to the saxophone students at a jazz clinic when their teacher asked for specific suggestions, “Play better.”
Joe Venuti quieting a noisy audience with one word growled over the microphone.
I’ll stop there, so I don’t spoil the surprises, but there are two hundred more moments in this book that made me shake my head in astonishment or stop reading because of the way Hank described someone, as a great novelist does, in a phrase. There are many melancholy moments, for more than a few of the people chronicled would not live on for decades more, but the overall mood of the book is joyous, not elegiac. I felt Hank’s delight when encountering a revered person or hearing a passionate performance.
And what is also remarkable and rare is Hank’s gracious candor. His portrait of John Hammond is the most memorable example of a clear-eyed yet affectionate perspective. It is easy to elevate Hammond, based on his own myth-making; it is easy to take aim at him as a fabulist. Hank nimbly balances the narrative between hagiography and character-assassination, adding details that few would have known. Fairness! So rare.
And the photographs! Hank learned a good deal from Berenice Abbott, and it shows. His candid photos are in focus, his posed ones don’t look stiff, and the people he photographed all look glad to have him aiming a camera, no small thing. Paintings, sketches, record labels, album covers also.
I don’t like ten-best lists and I think groceries come before records and books. However, there are exceptions, and **MORE THAN THE MUSIC** is one.

## A FEAST OF A BOOK: “MORE THAN THE MUSIC: A JAZZ MEMOIR by HANK O’NEAL” (TCU PRESS,2025)
A concert at Town Hall, November 28, 1959, with an extended performance of ONE O’CLOCK JUMP with Count Basie, John Coltrane, Milt Hinton, Elvin Jones, Lee Konitz, Bob Brookmeyer, and others.
Zoot Sims’ advice to the saxophone students at a jazz clinic when their teacher asked for specific suggestions, “Play better.”
Joe Venuti quieting a noisy audience with one word growled over the microphone.
I’ll stop there, so I don’t spoil the surprises, but there are two hundred more moments in this book that made me shake my head in astonishment or stop reading because of the way Hank described someone, as a great novelist does, in a phrase. There are many melancholy moments, for more than a few of the people chronicled would not live on for decades more, but the overall mood of the book is joyous, not elegiac. I felt Hank’s delight when encountering a revered person or hearing a passionate performance.
And what is also remarkable and rare is Hank’s gracious candor. His portrait of John Hammond is the most memorable example of a clear-eyed yet affectionate perspective. It is easy to elevate Hammond, based on his own myth-making; it is easy to take aim at him as a fabulist. Hank nimbly balances the narrative between hagiography and character-assassination, adding details that few would have known. Fairness! So rare.
And the photographs! Hank learned a good deal from Berenice Abbott, and it shows. His candid photos are in focus, his posed ones don’t look stiff, and the people he photographed all look glad to have him aiming a camera, no small thing. Paintings, sketches, record labels, album covers also.
I don’t like ten-best lists and I think groceries come before records and books. However, there are exceptions, and **MORE THAN THE MUSIC** is one.

## A FEAST OF A BOOK: “MORE THAN THE MUSIC: A JAZZ MEMOIR by HANK O’NEAL” (TCU PRESS,2025)
A concert at Town Hall, November 28, 1959, with an extended performance of ONE O’CLOCK JUMP with Count Basie, John Coltrane, Milt Hinton, Elvin Jones, Lee Konitz, Bob Brookmeyer, and others.
Zoot Sims’ advice to the saxophone students at a jazz clinic when their teacher asked for specific suggestions, “Play better.”
Joe Venuti quieting a noisy audience with one word growled over the microphone.
I’ll stop there, so I don’t spoil the surprises, but there are two hundred more moments in this book that made me shake my head in astonishment or stop reading because of the way Hank described someone, as a great novelist does, in a phrase. There are many melancholy moments, for more than a few of the people chronicled would not live on for decades more, but the overall mood of the book is joyous, not elegiac. I felt Hank’s delight when encountering a revered person or hearing a passionate performance.
And what is also remarkable and rare is Hank’s gracious candor. His portrait of John Hammond is the most memorable example of a clear-eyed yet affectionate perspective. It is easy to elevate Hammond, based on his own myth-making; it is easy to take aim at him as a fabulist. Hank nimbly balances the narrative between hagiography and character-assassination, adding details that few would have known. Fairness! So rare.
And the photographs! Hank learned a good deal from Berenice Abbott, and it shows. His candid photos are in focus, his posed ones don’t look stiff, and the people he photographed all look glad to have him aiming a camera, no small thing. Paintings, sketches, record labels, album covers also.
I don’t like ten-best lists and I think groceries come before records and books. However, there are exceptions, and **MORE THAN THE MUSIC** is one.

## A FEAST OF A BOOK: “MORE THAN THE MUSIC: A JAZZ MEMOIR by HANK O’NEAL” (TCU PRESS,2025)
In 1970, I had just started college and was working a part-time job that paid $1.85 an hour. Thanks to indulgent parents, I could make intermittent trips into New York City, ending in Greenwich Village, when thirty dollars could finance a gratifying solo outing for books and records. I bought lps that were entirely or partially his handiwork: pianists Bobby Henderson, Don Ewell; Eddie Condon Town Hall concerts, Bobby Hackett and Vic Dickenson, Ruby Braff, Ellis Larkins, and George Barnes . . . and on and on. There was the beginning of a renaissance in swing jazz at the time, not only expressed in gigs with players youthful and venerable, and recordings: Chiaroscuro was joined by MJR, Concord, and Pablo, among others.
In spring 1972, Hank was teaching a class in live recording at the New School, not far away on Twelfth Street. I recall a concert series (I may have the order wrong): Eddie Condon, Gene Krupa, Wild Bill Davison, and Dick Wellstood. (Hank says in the book that the budget for the concert was $400, but the musicians didn’t care.) A Ruby Braff concert with Milt Hinton, Sammy Margolis, Benny Aronov, and Dottie Dodgion; a piano roundtable with Eubie Blake, Claude Hopkins, Teddy Wilson, and Dill Jones; finally an Earl Hines solo recital capped by his monumental BOOGIE WOOGIE ON THE ST. LOUIS BLUES, with a tremolo that continued through twelve choruses.
I attended all four concerts, getting to the hall early enough to be the first or among the first on line, and taped them all with equipment barely hidden. That’s the source of the first musical interlude: music not included on the CD issue for reasons of length. If Hank saw me in the front row, in one case with a reel-to-reel recorder on my lap, he didn’t fuss. I continued to purchase Chairoscuro records, then CDs.
